content: Lignite, commonly known as brown coal, represents the lowest rank of coal and is predominantly utilized as a fuel source for steam-electric power generation. It is characterized by its brownish-black appearance and possesses a notably high inherent moisture content, which can reach up to 66%. Additionally, it contains a significantly higher ash content compared to bituminous coal. Lignite is a complex and heterogeneous mixture of organic compounds, making it impossible to define its structure with a single chemical formula. In the United States, the average heat content of lignite consumed is approximately 13 million Btu per ton (15 MJ/kg) on an as-received basis, which includes both its inherent moisture and mineral matter. When lignite is chemically treated with quaternary amines, it forms a compound known as amine-treated lignite (ATL). This modified form of lignite is employed in oil well drilling fluids to minimize fluid loss during drilling operations. Due to its low energy density, lignite is inefficient to transport over long distances, which limits its trade on the global market compared to higher-grade coals. Consequently, lignite is often combusted in power plants located in close proximity to the mining sites. A notable example of this practice is observed in the Latrobe Valley of Australia. The combustion of lignite in power plants results in significantly higher carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions compared to plants that utilize black coal. The continued use of lignite-fired power plants, particularly when combined with strip mining and in the absence of carbon capture and storage technologies, remains a subject of political and environmental debate.
